verdicts.evidence: Tell students that they will now review their Sky notebooks and pick two entries to share with the visitors.

clauses.clause: Refer to specific techniques, topics, modes, and genres that resonate most

verdicts.evidence: 'What part of your poem are you most proud and most excited to share with a visitor?' (Responses will vary.)
verdicts.rationale: The lesson includes a moment where students discuss a personal preference about their own writing: "What part of your poem are you most proud and most excited to share with a visitor?" This touches on a personal writing preference, partially meeting the first clause. However, the discussion is narrowly about pride in a specific product (the poem), not about broader reading and writing preferences. The second clause — referring to specific techniques, topics, modes, or genres that resonate most — is not met: no activity asks students to name or reflect on preferred techniques, topics, modes, or genres. The lesson is focused on presentation preparation, not on articulating reading/writing preferences.

verdicts.evidence: Using a total participation technique, invite responses from the group: 'What should you keep in mind while you are selecting entries from your Sky notebook to share? What criteria should those entries meet?' (neat writing, accurate information, entries that show different information and times of day)
verdicts.rationale: In Work Time A, students develop and apply knowledge of audience (visitors) and purpose (to teach about the sun, moon, and stars) to select Sky notebook entries to share. Students respond to the question about what criteria entries should meet (neat writing, accurate information, entries showing different information and times of day), demonstrating their understanding of purpose. Students then review their own notebooks and select two entries, evaluating which entries best achieve the purpose of teaching visitors based on quality and content criteria. All three clauses are met through this selection and evaluation process.

clauses.clause: Work with others to investigate questions (I/C)
Work with others to solve problems (I/C)
Work with others to explore and create texts (I/C)

verdicts.evidence: Guide students through four rounds of the protocol using the following questions: 'What is a pattern that the sun, moon, or stars follow? How would you describe that pattern?' 'What is something you learned about the sun, moon, or stars that you did not know before?' 'What do you still wonder about the sun, moon, or stars?'
verdicts.rationale: The "discuss topics" clause is met: during Work Time B, students use the Back-to-Back and Face-to-Face protocol to discuss sun, moon, and stars topics with a partner ("Guide students through four rounds of the protocol using the following questions: 'What is a pattern that the sun, moon, or stars follow?'…"). Students also share out with the whole group afterward. However, the remaining clauses are not met. Students do not collaboratively investigate questions — the protocol has them answer pre-set teacher questions, not pursue inquiry together. There is no collaborative problem-solving activity. Students do not collaboratively explore or create texts — they individually select notebook entries and individually practice reading their already-completed poems aloud to a partner (sharing, not co-creating). The lesson is preparation for a celebration, not collaborative text creation or investigation.
verdicts.grounding_note: evidence quote found in lesson raw text

clauses.note: Students use their Sky notebooks and module texts to build knowledge about the sun, moon, and stars, then actively share that information and ideas with partners during the Back-to-Back and Face-to-Face protocol and Pinky Partners protocol, satisfying the 'share information and ideas' and 'build knowledge' purposes.

verdicts.evidence: 'What is something you learned about the sun, moon, or stars that you did not know before?' … Invite a few students to share out what they discussed with their partners during the protocol.
verdicts.rationale: The standard's four purposes (build knowledge, develop skills, make informed decisions, share information and ideas) form an OR list; any one student-performed purpose satisfies the clause. Students make use of their module texts (Sky notebooks, "What the Sun Sees" poems) to share information and ideas about the sun, moon, and stars with partners. In Work Time B, students discuss questions such as "What is something you learned about the sun, moon, or stars that you did not know before?" and "What is a pattern that the sun, moon, or stars follow? How would you describe that pattern?" — actively using texts to build and share knowledge. In Work Time C, students read their poems aloud to a partner via the Pinky Partners protocol, again sharing information drawn from texts. The student is the actor throughout: selecting notebook entries, discussing content with partners, and presenting poems aloud.
